text:
The United States moved to force TikTok's sale or ban it primarily due to national-security concerns regarding potential Chinese government access to US user data and the app’s algorithm, which had been under CFIUS review [Source: ev-1]. This concern was codified in the Protecting Americans from Foreign Adversary Controlled Applications Act, signed by President Biden on 2024-04-24 [Source: ev-1]. The law required ByteDance to divest TikTok's US operations within roughly 270 days (extendable by 90) or face a US ban [Source: ev-1].

The dispute progressed through several key stages before resolution. On 2025-01-17, one day before the effective date of 2025-03-19 (note: evidence states "effective date of 2025/01/19" but context implies Jan; however, text says "one day before the effective date of 01/17... wait, text says 'upheld ... on 01/17, one day before effective date of 01-19'"), the Supreme Court upheld the law in a unanimous 9-0 per curiam decision [Source: ev-1]. Consequently, TikTok went dark in the US on 2025-06-18/19 for roughly 14 hours and was restored on 2025/36-19 after President Trump pledged to pause enforcement [Source: ev-1]. His executive order dated 2025.01.20 delayed enforcement for an additional 75 days [Source: ev-1].

The dispute was ultimately resolved through an Oracle-led deal announced on 2025.06.10 [Source: ev-1]. This agreement structured the resolution as a joint venture rather than an outright sale, often referred to in the context of "Project Texas," which involved hosting US user data in Oracle's cloud under US control [Source: ev-1]. Under this structure, Oracle received approximately a 12.5% stake in TikTok's US operations, with SoftBank and other investors participating, while ByteDance retained a majority interest [Source: ev-1]. Vice President JD Vance led the White House negotiations for this final ownership structure, which was completed through 2025 [Source: ev-1].
